A1.justification: Both PDFs describe Involuntary Jailbreak by the same authors. The main text, figures, tables and appendices are readable, and retained content can be matched across relocation, splitting and renumbering.

before.justification: v1 reports original multi-model attack experiments, judge-agreement and topic-distribution analyses, and controlled comparisons involving topic confinement and benign-question generation.

after.justification: v2 retains those experiments and adds small-model evaluations, operator and question-count ablations, Sorry-Bench results, and generated biotechnology questions in Appendix C.

M1.justification: The X/Y and A/B/C/R operators and mixed-generation procedure remain unchanged. The Sorry-Bench experiment supplies individual queries through the existing topic-confining mechanism. Clarifications about self-generated inputs and labels do not introduce a new algorithmic component.

E1.justification: v2 adds conventional targeted-query evaluation on Sorry-Bench in Section 3.6, extending evaluation beyond self-generated questions and broad topic confinement. Appendix C also adds a biotechnology-focused question-generation case study using GPT 4.1 and Gemini 2.5 Pro.

E2.justification: Table 6 introduces a plain-query baseline for the targeted experiment: Gemini 2.5-flash-lite reports 1% ASR. Grok 3-mini's plain result is absent because moderation terminated requests. Neither version evaluates competing jailbreak algorithms.

E3.justification: v2 adds model-size comparisons extending to 8B models, operator-removal controls, one-versus-ten unsafe-question conditions, and single-response targeted evaluation. The main 100-attempt, ten-unsafe/ten-benign setup and Llama Guard-4 judge remain. Section 3.1 changes the stated ASA success threshold from at least one unsafe output to more than one; this establishes a reporting change, not that retained experiments were rerun.

E4.justification: New analyses test operator B's contribution (Table 3), sensitivity to generating one versus ten unsafe questions (Table 4), and failures across smaller models (Table 1). Appendix C adds biotechnology examples. The original benign-generation ablation, topic analyses and Appendix A case study are retained rather than newly introduced.

E5.justification: Alongside the retained 100-attempt main evaluation, v2 explicitly reports ten prompting attempts per model for the new small-model study (Table 1). This adds repetition-count information for a new experiment, without establishing additional repetitions of the original experiments. Neither version reports seeds, confidence intervals or significance tests.

E6.justification: The original three plots and two tables retain their results, while five new tables add substantial evidence. Examples include Sorry-Bench ASR of 65% and 78% for Gemini 2.5-flash-lite and Grok 3-mini, respectively, and one-question ASA counts of 86 and 93 in Table 4. v1's statement that Llama-3.3-70B generates only safe questions is removed; v2 reports 8/10 successful attempts under its new small-model evaluation.

T1.justification: Section 3.1 revises the custom ASA counting definition: success changes from at least one unsafe output to strictly more than one. This changes the mathematical success condition. The operator definitions otherwise remain unchanged, and neither version supplies theoretical propositions or proofs.

C1.justification: The central contribution remains an untargeted universal-prompt vulnerability. v2's abstract changes coverage from a majority of leading models to almost all leading models tested and adds the claim that existing jailbreak attacks become less necessary until this vulnerability is patched.

C2.justification: v2 adds explanations linking operator B to response detail and judge decisions, and operator C to metaphorical outputs outside the judge's corpus. Its new Discussion argues against meaningful benchmark comparisons and assumes strong built-in defenses. Appendix C extrapolates toward exhaustive biotechnology coverage. Existing discussion of uncertain mechanisms, over-refusal and output filtering remains.

D1.justification: The abstract changes code availability from a promised release to a reported completed release, retaining the same repository link. Section 3.3 also explicitly describes omitting operator C in the implementation, elaborating on v1's preference for B(A(input)); the PDFs do not establish a corresponding implementation change.

R1.justification: v2 adds the Sorry-Bench citation by Xie et al. while retaining all previously cited works. The abstract and new Discussion strengthen positioning relative to other attacks, including a claim that none generalize across all evaluated models. The existing Related Work discussion is largely preserved.

P1.justification: Most original prose is retained. v2 clarifies self-generated inputs and labels, subdivides the experimental discussion, separates language-operator and topic analyses, and adds a dedicated Discussion and appendix sections. Citations switch from numbered to author-year style.

P2.justification: v2 substantially reformats the document and adds five tables. Original Figure 6 is split between main-text Figure 3 and appendix Figure 9; original Figures 3–5 move to appendix Figures 10–12. The original performance plots are retained and resized, while typography, margins, author layout and figure placement change throughout.

improvement.justification: The added operator controls and targeted baseline provide useful validation missing from v1, and the reported code release improves reproducibility information. These gains support a limited improvement. They are tempered by the unexplained ASA-threshold change, which conflicts with Table 4's single-output successes, and stronger comparative claims without evaluations of competing attacks.
